replacements.15: Grapevine phenology determines the seasonal timing of vegetative growth and reproduction and the environmental conditions experienced during development. Accurate estimates provide a temporal basis for vineyard monitoring and regional assessments of environmental exposure. Long-term observations document earlier development in European vineyards and earlier maturity in Australian growing regions (Tomasi et al., 2011; Webb et al., 2011). The consequences vary among stages: budburst timing affects exposure to spring frost, whereas shifts in ripening alter the temperature and moisture conditions experienced by berries (Sgubin et al., 2018; Cook and Wolkovich, 2016). These relationships motivate regional phenology prediction; frost damage, water demand and management outcomes are distinct endpoints requiring additional evaluation.
replacements.16: Thermal accumulation provides a practical basis for predicting developmental dates. The Grapevine Flowering Veraison model uses heat accumulation above a base temperature to predict flowering and veraison (Parker et al., 2011), with cultivar-specific requirements accounting for substantial timing differences (Parker et al., 2013). Veraison and maturity/harvest also reflect source–sink conditions, water availability and management (Sadras and Moran, 2013; Webb et al., 2012). Harvest dates and attainment of a specified berry sugar concentration represent different endpoints (Parker et al., 2020). Regional models must therefore accommodate both developmental responses and heterogeneity in the observed stages.
replacements.17: Selecting an appropriate process structure is a prerequisite for regional prediction. Forcing-only models accumulate heat from a prescribed origin, whereas chilling–forcing models represent winter cold exposure followed by, or overlapping with, forcing (Chuine, 2000; Chuine and Régnière, 2017). Linear and nonlinear temperature responses provide another structural choice. Greater complexity has not consistently improved grapevine predictions (García de Cortázar-Atauri et al., 2009; Fila et al., 2014), and recent Australian and Bordeaux evaluations show that response-function rankings depend on the sampled environments and model formulation (Thomas et al., 2026; de Rességuier et al., 2026). Controlled component comparisons are consequently needed to identify useful regional structures and distinguish forcing, chilling and interaction effects.
replacements.20: Temperature representativeness provides a separate opportunity for improvement. Gridded weather supports spatially consistent regional modelling but resolves terrain more coarsely than individual vineyards (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021). Vineyard measurements reveal spatial variability in meteorological conditions (Matese et al., 2014), and local phenology applications demonstrate the value of spatially resolved temperature inputs (de Rességuier et al., 2026; Fonseca et al., 2025). A digital elevation model (DEM) permits a transparent adjustment for site-to-grid elevation differences. Its predictive benefit nevertheless requires evaluation after model recalibration because a fixed lapse rate cannot represent inversions, seasonal gradients or other sources of local temperature variation.
replacements.18: Residual learning offers further improvement by estimating systematic errors that remain after process simulation. Hybrid modelling combines mechanistic structure with statistical flexibility (Reichstein et al., 2019), with applications in terrestrial evaporation and crop phenology (Koppa et al., 2022; Ou et al., 2025). The residual model developed here combines simulated developmental states, recent temperature histories, photoperiod and terrain to adjust predicted event dates. This design provides environmental context beyond shared thermal requirements while retaining the process model as the developmental baseline. It may also capture discrepancies related to temperature representativeness, so its gains need not add to those from DEM correction. Evaluation across the same structures and observations can establish the extra predictive value of each correction without attributing residuals to specific biological or physical mechanisms.
replacements.19: Validation must match the regional prediction task. Repeated observations and sites sharing weather cells can create dependence between calibration and testing (Roberts et al., 2017). Holding out complete site groups evaluates prediction at unobserved sites within represented thermal environments. This setting supports retrospective estimation with realized weather; independent regional transfer and operational forecasting require separate tests.
replacements.21: The objectives were to identify the best-performing process structure for regional grapevine phenology prediction, quantify further improvement from DEM-based temperature correction, and evaluate the new residual model and its combined benefit with temperature correction. Ten process structures, two temperature inputs and the presence or absence of residual learning were evaluated on common calibration–test partitions. Both improvements were assessed across all ten structures, allowing process-model selection, final hybrid accuracy and overlapping correction gains to be distinguished.
